newsitem.title: MALTA: Confusion as Malta replaces VAT with new system.
newsitem.headline: Confusion as Malta replaces VAT with new system.

text.p: Malta on Tuesday abolished its much disliked Value Added Tax, replacing it with a system of customs and excise duties to fulfill a pledge widely credited with having won the Labour Party last October's general election.
Local radios reported wide confusion over the introduction following a row between retailers and government over adjusting fiscal cash registers.
"Nobody can understand what's happening," said a frustrated Maltese resident. "Shopkeepers have been advised neither to raise their prices nor lower them until everything is sorted out."

VAT was introduced by the Nationalist government on January 1, 1995 as Malta geared up to join the European Union. It was strongly disliked by traditionally-secretive family retailers who saw it as intrusive.
The then-opposition Labour Party said it raised the cost of living and promised to repeal it.

After the party's victory last October, Prime Minister Alfred Sant froze Malta's application to join the EU and proposed a three-tier system incorporating import duties, an excise tax on products and an excise tax on services, to replace VAT.
But its introduction has brought a flood of complaints.
The Chamber of Commerce said the economy was characterized by "an environment of confusion and uncertainty" with the coming into force of the new system.
Malta's Association of General Retailers and Traders (GRTU) protested that retailers would have to pay duties for stock already in hand, saying that could create cash flow problems.
Under VAT those duties would have been recovered when the products were sold to consumers.

The association also insists the government should pay for modifications on cash registers to operate the new system. The government says owners should pay because they would eventually benefit through the new system through fewer compliance costs.
The GRTU has directed its members not to adjust their cash registers until agreement is reached.
Under the new system, import duties from the European Union, with which Malta carries out 75 percent of its trade, have been retained at 15 percent as under VAT.

Imports from outside the EU are charged an additional eight percent. Most imported products will also be subject to a five percent excise tax. Imported raw materials for exporting industry, agriculture and essential items such as medicines are not taxed.
The opposition Nationalist Party says the system is just "a bad copy of VAT" because it retains the essential elements of VAT but confuses its implementation.
Prime Minister Sant says the new system will benefit small traders, who will not be taxed if they do not exceed certain turnover thresholds, and will not increase the cost of living.
He argues that some 41,000 retailers will now no longer collect tax for the government since excise duty on products will be collected by wholesalers.
The cost of services -- anything from cable television and car repairs to a haircut - will now be charged five percent excise duty instead of 15 percent VAT.
But Malta Federation of Industry in a sharply worded statement late on Monday said the government had rushed the new system through and was threatening the future of industry.
It said exporting industry would be saddled with additional costs of some three percent, particularly because tax on services was not refundable as under VAT.

The Nationalist Party says Labour won the election not because it promised to remove VAT, but because thousands of retailers thought its removal would also bring the end of fiscal cash registers which include an electronic memory that can be checked by tax inspectors.
The new government has kept the cash registers and encourages consumers to demand fiscal receipts by introducing a lottery with receipts serving tickets.
